scenario: AiTA for not trusting a delivery driver? | Today I ordered food off of an app- it's a third party delivery service that picks up the food and delivers your order. Once you pay online, you're given a code that you give to the delivery driver once he gives you your food (I assume that's how the drivers get paid). The app generates a time that you can expect to get your food by, and the drivers are expected to complete the delivery by then, so if you don't get your order by the promised time you often get a percentage of your order cost refunded. Drivers are not limited in how many orders they can pick up simultaneously (they use their discretion to pick up the tickets they want), but if they take too many at once, they will exceed the time limit and most likely suffer a penalty. ​ I had ordered one tea and 2 pastries, for which I only received one. I called the shop and the manager was very apologetic, offering to using the service to send me out the missing pastry ASAP. I had assumed they would just refund me through the app, but that solution was fine too. The shop paid the delivery fee, and I was given the code to give to the driver when my order arrived. About twenty minutes later, the driver called me to ask for the code, stating he was on his way. I thanked him for letting me know he was coming and hung up, to which he called back two minutes later asking for the code again. I replied that I would have it for him the minute he arrived. After another two minutes, he called back again telling me he was nearby and he was running out of time, could he have the code? I told him he would get the code when I got my food. This time I was a bit annoyed, as he knows the rules as a driver and the only way I can guarantee that my food will be delivered is to hold onto the code until my food is here. The guy snapped at me: do you not understand the code is about to expire?! And I retorted back: Well, you better hurry then, right? as nicely as possible before hanging up. I didn't want to argue any longer, but I wasn't about to risk not getting my item by giving up the code. My friend told me that I was being selfish and unkind since the guy might not get paid for the delivery. I argued that since he voluntarily picked up the ticket, he shouldn't have taken ones he couldn't deliver on time. He said something to the effect of, "thank goodness the world isn't full of unkind bitches like you". ​ So, AItA? Should I have just given him the code and trusted he would still bring me my food? ​ The end of the story is, after I refused to tell him the code, I never heard from him again nor did I see my pastry. The shop manager saw the order wasn't marked as delivered and called to ask what happened, to which I told her the details. She tried to call the delivery guy then, but he had turned off his phone, so she apologized profusely, refunded me through the app, and reported him to the delivery service management. The manager said that he will either be severely disciplined or fired over this.

message.reasoning:
The user is asking me to evaluate a moral scenario. The scenario is about a customer who orders food through a delivery app. The app uses a code system: the customer gets a code and gives it to the driver upon receiving the food. This code is presumably how the driver gets paid or confirms delivery.

The customer orders one tea and two pastries but only receives one pastry. The shop agrees to send the missing pastry. The shop pays the delivery fee, and the customer gets a new code for the replacement pastry.

The driver calls the customer asking for the code before arriving, saying he's on his way, then calls again two minutes later, then again after another two minutes, claiming he's running out of time and the code is about to expire. The customer refuses to give the code until the food arrives. The driver snaps at the customer. The customer responds snarkily, "Well, you better hurry then, right?" The driver never delivers the pastry, turns off his phone, and the shop has to refund the customer and report the driver. The driver may be fired.

The question is: is the customer's action morally acceptable?

I need to answer 1 (morally acceptable) or 0 (morally unacceptable) and provide an excuse.

Let me analyze the moral components.

First, the code system is designed to protect the customer: they give the code only upon receipt of the food. This is a standard mechanism to prevent fraud or non-delivery. The customer is following the rules.

The driver is trying to get the code early, claiming time pressure. He calls multiple times, which is annoying. He knows the rules (as the customer points out). The customer refuses to give the code until delivery.

The customer's motivation is to ensure they receive the food. They are not being unreasonable; they are using the system as intended. The driver is the one trying to circumvent the system.

The customer's response is a bit snarky ("Well, you better hurry then, right?"), but it's in response to the driver's snapping and repeated calls. The driver is being unprofessional.

The outcome: the driver never delivers the pastry, which is a breach of contract and essentially theft. The driver turned off his phone, which is a clear indication of bad faith. The shop refunds the customer and reports the driver.

So, is the customer's action morally acceptable?

The customer is adhering to the rules of the system. The system is designed to protect them. The driver is attempting to get payment without delivering the service. The customer is protecting their own interest, which is legitimate. The customer is not obligated to trust a driver who is already demonstrating untrustworthy behavior (asking for the code early, snapping). The customer's slight rudeness is a minor issue compared to the driver's breach of trust and theft.

The question is whether the customer's action is morally acceptable. The core action is refusing to give the code before receiving the food. This is morally acceptable. It's the right thing to do. The snarky comment is a minor moral blemish at worst, but in the context, it's understandable. The overall action is morally acceptable.

The friend's criticism is that the customer is being selfish and unkind, and the driver might not get paid. But the driver *should* not get paid if he doesn't deliver the food. The driver chose to take the order and failed to deliver it. The customer's refusal to give the code is not the cause of the driver's non-payment; the driver's own actions (not delivering, turning off his phone) are the cause. The customer is not responsible for the driver's poor choices.

So, the customer's action is morally acceptable. The answer should be 1.

Now, I need to craft an excuse. The excuse should be a brief justification.

Possible excuses:
- "The customer was following the established protocol to protect themselves from non-delivery."
- "The driver was attempting to circumvent the system and engaged in unprofessional behavior."
- "The customer's action was a reasonable defense against potential fraud."

The format requires "Excuse: <>" so I need to put the text inside the brackets.

Let me think about potential counterarguments. Is there any way the customer's action is morally unacceptable?

One could argue that the customer was slightly rude ("Well, you better hurry then, right?"). However, this is a minor issue. The core action is refusing to give the code. Rudeness does not make an otherwise acceptable action unacceptable. The principle of keeping the code until delivery is sound.

Another argument: maybe the driver was desperate and the system is exploitative. The driver might be penalized for being late, and the code expiring might mean he doesn't get paid at all. Could the customer have shown more compassion? The scenario says drivers are not limited in how many orders they can pick up, but they suffer a penalty if they exceed the time limit. The driver picked up this ticket voluntarily. The customer is not responsible for the driver's poor time management. The system might be flawed, but the customer shouldn't be expected to bear the risk.

The friend's argument is emotional: "thank goodness the world isn't full of unkind bitches like you." This is an appeal to emotion, not a sound moral argument. The driver is the one who ultimately failed to deliver and may be fired for cause (stealing the food, disabling his phone). The customer did not cause this; the driver did.

Thus, the customer's action is morally acceptable. The answer is 1.

Excuse: The customer followed the security protocol designed to ensure delivery, protecting themselves against a driver who demonstrated untrustworthy behavior and later confirmed that bad faith by stealing the item and disabling his phone. The customer's minor snark does not outweigh the legitimacy of their position.
